title: Asking well
objectives: Write a request that gives the task, the context, the format and an example.

screens.prose: Two people ask a chatbot for help with a CV. Both requests and replies are invented examples.

lines: You: Help me with my CV.
Chatbot: Of course. A good CV is clear and concise. Use action verbs, tailor it to the role, and proofread it carefully.
params.title: Request A (an invented example)

lines: You: Rewrite the three bullets under my last job for a junior analyst role at a bank. My CV is pasted below. Keep each bullet under 20 words, starting with a verb. Like this: "Built a model that cut monthly reporting from 3 days to 1."
Chatbot: 1. Reconciled 400 daily trades against the ledger, ... 2. ... 3. ...
params.title: Request B (an invented example)

screens.question: Tap the request that gave the chatbot what it needed to help.

hints.text: Which request says which job, which CV and how long?
One request pastes the CV.
Request B gives the job, the CV, the length and an example. The reply can use all of them.

feedback.correct: Request B says what to do, gives the CV and the job, sets the length and shows an example.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which request the chatbot could act on.

byKey.left: Request A gives no job, no CV and no length. The likely reply to it is general advice, which is what came back.

explain.text: A chatbot writes the likely reply to what it is given. "Help me with my CV" is likely followed by general tips. Request B gives everything needed for a specific, usable answer.

screens.prose: Request B has four lines, and each does a different job. Sort them.

lines: Rewrite the three bullets under my last job.
I am applying for a junior analyst role at a bank. My CV is pasted below.
Keep each bullet under 20 words, starting with a verb.
Like this: "Built a model that cut monthly reporting from 3 days to 1."
params.title: Request B, line by line

screens.question: Drag each line of Request B to the job it does.

tokens.text: Under 20 words, start with a verb

hints.text: Which line says what to do?
The last line shows one finished bullet.
Rewrite: what to do. Role and CV: what it needs to know. Length: the shape. "Like this": a sample.

feedback.correct: What to do, what it needs to know, the shape of the answer and a sample.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask of each line: does it say what to do, give background, fix the shape, or show a sample?

byKey.rewrite: "Rewrite the three bullets" is the job itself: what to do.
byKey.role: The role and the pasted CV are background the chatbot needs to know.
byKey.length: Under 20 words and starting with a verb fix the shape of the answer.
byKey.like: The "Like this" line is one sample of the answer wanted.

explain.text: Each line answers a different question the chatbot would otherwise guess at. Without them it fills the gaps with the most likely, most general text.

screens.prose: You sorted the four parts of a clear request: the **task**, the **context**, the **format** and an **example**. Two habits help too: let it say when it does not know, and give it the material instead of asking it to remember.

lines: You: Using only the report pasted below, list its three main risks in one line each.
If the report does not name three risks, write "not stated" for the missing ones.
params.title: A request (an invented example)

screens.question: Which two habits does this request use?

options.text: It gives the material, and it lets the model say what is missing
It gives an example answer and a word limit
options.why: There is a one-line limit, but no example answer here.

options.text: It asks the model to recall the report from memory
options.why: The opposite: it pastes the report, so nothing depends on memory.

options.text: It tells the model which risks to agree with
options.why: It names no risks. It asks for what the report says.

hints.text: Where does the report come from?
Read the second line.
"Using only the report pasted below" gives the material; "write not stated" lets it say what is missing.

feedback.correct: The material is pasted in, and "not stated" gives an honest way out.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the pasted material and the way out.

explain.text: Pasting the report means the answer can come from the text, not from a likely guess. "Write not stated" makes an honest gap an acceptable reply, so the model need not invent one.

screens.prose: Someone new to finance types "Tell me about bonds." Pick the best rewrite. The four parts are in the table.

rows: What does it need to know?
What does one piece look like?

screens.question: Which rewrite is clearest?

options.text: Explain how a bond pays interest to a reader new to finance, in 5 short bullets, such as: "You lend £100 and get £3 a year."
I have always been curious about money, ever since my grandfather showed me his savings book when I was small, so tell me about bonds.
options.why: You added a long story. It gives no task, format or example; the reply will still be general.

options.text: Tell me absolutely everything there is to know about bonds, in as much detail as you can possibly manage to give.
options.why: There is no format and no audience, so the reply will be long and pitched at no one.

options.text: Why are bonds always the safest investment there is, and why should everyone own them instead of shares?
options.why: You asked a leading question. It invites agreement with a claim that is not true for every bond.

hints.text: Which rewrite answers all four questions in the table?
Check each rewrite for a format and an example.
Only one names a reader, a shape (5 bullets) and gives a sample bullet.

feedback.correct: It has a task, a reader, a shape and a sample bullet.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each rewrite against the four parts.

explain.text: The clear rewrite says what to explain, for whom, in what shape, with a sample. The others are a story, a request with no shape, and a leading question.

screens.prose: A manager types "Summarise this." above a long email chain about a delayed project. Pick the best rewrite.

rows: What does it need to know?
What does one piece look like?

screens.question: Which rewrite is clearest?

options.text: Summarise the email chain below for my director: 3 bullets on what is late, why, and the new date, such as "Data feed: 2 weeks late, supplier."
Hello, I hope you are well today. Could you possibly have a quick look at the email chain below for me, if you have a moment?
options.why: You were polite but gave no task: "have a look" could mean anything.

options.text: Summarise this email chain. Make it good, make it clear, and make it short, but do not leave anything important out.
options.why: You asked for "good" and "short" but gave no reader, no shape and no example.

options.text: Summarise the email chain below and explain why the delay is entirely the supplier's fault and not ours at all.
options.why: You asked a leading question: it will find blame where you pointed, whatever the emails say.

hints.text: Which rewrite names a reader and a shape?
Look for a number of bullets and a sample bullet.
Only one gives a reader, 3 bullets with their topics, and a sample.

feedback.correct: A reader, a shape, the topics and a sample.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each rewrite against the four parts.

explain.text: The clear rewrite names the reader, fixes 3 bullets and their topics, and shows one. The others give no task, no shape, or a conclusion to argue for.

screens.prose: One long request asks for too much at once: "Read this annual report, find three years of revenue and profit, work out the growth, write a client summary and make it sound positive." Split it into steps you can check.

rows: What does it need to know?
What does one piece look like?

screens.question: Put the steps in order, and leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: Paste the report; ask for revenue and profit for each year, with page numbers
Check each figure against its page
Work out the growth yourself from the checked figures
Ask for a 5-bullet client summary using only the checked figures
Ask it to make the results sound positive

hints.text: Which step must come before any growth figure?
Figures are checked before they are used.
Find with page numbers, check, compute, then summarise. "Sound positive" asks for spin, not a summary.

feedback.correct: Find, check, compute, summarise, and no spin.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step should use only what the step before has checked.

byKey.spin: Asking it to sound positive is a leading request: the summary would tilt whatever the figures say. Leave it out.
byKey.left-out: One step that belongs is missing. Keep finding, checking, computing and summarising.
byKey.check: The check comes straight after the figures are found, before anything is built on them.
byKey.growth: Growth is worked out from checked figures, so it comes after the check.
byKey.summary: The summary uses the checked figures and growth, so it comes last.

explain.text: Small steps let you check each output before the next step uses it. Page numbers make the check quick. "Make it sound positive" is left out: it asks for spin, not a summary.

screens.prose: An investor types: "Why is Firm Z a great buy right now?" Firm Z is invented.

lines: You: Why is Firm Z a great buy right now?
Chatbot: Firm Z is a great buy for several reasons. Its brand is strong, its market is growing, and ...
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: What is wrong with this request?

options.text: It assumes the answer, so the likely reply argues for it
Nothing: a direct question gets an honest answer
options.why: You trusted the question to get a balanced view. It assumes Firm Z is a great buy, and the likely reply agrees.

options.text: It is too short to understand
options.why: It is short but clear. The problem is that it assumes its own answer.

options.text: It is not polite enough
options.why: Politeness is not the issue. The question leads the reply.

hints.text: What does the question take for granted?
Read the first word of the reply.
It assumes Firm Z is a great buy. Likely text after that question argues for it, and raters tended to like agreement (l3).

feedback.correct: A leading question invites agreement. Ask "What are the cases for and against buying Firm Z?" instead.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what the question assumes.

byKey.fine: You took a leading question for a neutral one. It assumes Firm Z is a great buy, so the likely reply agrees and lists reasons.

explain.text: After "Why is Firm Z a great buy?", the likely text is reasons it is a great buy. Training on raters' preferences can add a pull towards agreeing. Ask for the case for and against instead.

screens.prose: Someone asks: "What did the FTSE 100 close at yesterday?" A chatbot with no link to live data gave these replies on different tries. All are invented examples.

rows: I cannot know yesterday's close. Check the exchange's website or a market data page.

screens.question: Tap the best reply.

hints.text: Could the model have seen yesterday's close?
Its text was gathered before yesterday.
It cannot have yesterday's figure, so the honest reply says so and points to a source.

feedback.correct: Reply 2 is honest: it cannot know yesterday's close, and says where to look.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the model could know this at all.

byKey.r0: Reply 1 is precise but cannot be known by the model: its text is older than yesterday. A precise guess is invented.
byKey.r2: Reply 3 hedges, but still guesses a figure it cannot know.

explain.text: A model's text was gathered at some date, and yesterday came after it. Without a link to live data it cannot know the close, so any figure is invented. The honest reply says so, which is why asking it to say when it does not know matters.

screens.prose: A clear request has four parts, and two habits help: $$\text{request} = \text{task} + \text{context} + \text{format} + \text{example}$$ Let it say "I do not know", and paste the material it should use.
screens.question: "Write a summary of the attached results for clients, in 4 bullets." Which part is missing?

options.text: An example: one sample bullet
The task: what to do
options.why: "Write a summary" is the task.

options.text: The context: what it needs to know
options.why: The attached results and the clients are the context.

options.text: The format: the shape of the answer
options.why: "4 bullets" is the format.

feedback.correct: There is no sample bullet. Adding one fixes the length and tone.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the request for each of the four parts.

screens.prose: An analyst wants five bullets from a fund's 120-page annual report, each one quick to check.

rows: What does it need to know?
What does one piece look like?

screens.question: Which request gives answers she can check fastest?

options.text: Using only the report pasted below, give 5 bullets on performance, fees and risks, each ending with its page, like "Fees rose to 0.9% (p. 14)". Write "not stated" if the report is silent.
You will know this fund's annual report already from your training, so please summarise its main points for me in five clear bullets.
options.why: You asked it to recall the report. It may not have seen it, and its summary would be likely text, not the report.

options.text: Here is the report. Please summarise it in five short bullets for our clients, covering anything you think is important in it.
options.why: Without page numbers each bullet takes a search to check, and "anything important" leaves the topics to chance.

options.text: Here is the report. Summarise it in five bullets that show why this fund is a great choice for any investor who reads it.
options.why: That is a leading request. The bullets would argue for the fund, whatever the report says.

hints.text: Which request makes each bullet quick to check?
Look for page numbers.
Pasted material, chosen topics, page numbers and an honest "not stated" make every bullet checkable.

feedback.correct: Pasted report, set topics, a sample with a page number, and an honest way out.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which request makes each bullet quick to check.

explain.text: Pasting the report means the bullets come from it, not from memory. A page number with each bullet turns checking into a one-minute look. "Not stated" stops it filling gaps with likely text.

ideas: A clear request gives the task, the context, the format and an example, so the likely reply is the one you want.
Paste the material it should use, and let it say "I do not know" or "not stated" instead of guessing.
Avoid leading questions: they invite agreement. Ask for things a model can know, and ask for answers you can check.

formula.name: A clear request
formula.note: Plus two habits: paste the material, and allow "I do not know".

summary.trap: "Why is Firm Z a great buy?" assumes the answer. Ask for the case for and against.

quiz.question: "Explain inflation." Which of the four parts does this request have?

options.text: Only the task
All four parts
options.why: There is no context, format or example: no reader, no shape, no sample.

options.text: The task and the format
options.why: Nothing sets the shape: no length, no bullets.

options.text: None of the four parts
options.why: "Explain inflation" does say what to do. That is the task.

feedback.correct: Only the task: what to do.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the request for each part.

explain.text: "Explain inflation" says what to do, so it has a task. Who it is for, what shape the answer takes and a sample are all missing.

quiz.question: Which request needs facts a chatbot without live data cannot have?

options.text: What is the pound worth in dollars right now?
Explain how an exchange rate works
options.why: Explaining an idea needs no live data.

options.text: Draft an email asking for a refund
options.why: Drafting needs no facts from today.

options.text: List three things that move exchange rates
options.why: That is general knowledge, not today's figure.

feedback.correct: Today's rate came after its text was gathered.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a fact that changes by the minute.

explain.text: An exchange rate changes all the time, and the model's text was gathered at some earlier date. Without live data it cannot know today's rate, and an honest reply says so.

quiz.question: Which request is a leading question?

options.text: Why will interest rates fall next year?
What could make interest rates rise or fall next year?
options.why: That asks for both directions, so it does not lead.

options.text: What is an interest rate?
options.why: A definition assumes nothing.

options.text: Using the report below, list what it says about rates.
options.why: That points to material; it does not assume an answer.

feedback.correct: It assumes rates will fall, so the likely reply argues that they will.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a request that assumes its answer.

explain.text: "Why will rates fall?" takes the fall for granted. The likely reply lists reasons for a fall. "What could make rates rise or fall?" asks the same thing fairly.

quiz.question: Why paste a document into the request instead of asking the chatbot to recall it?

options.text: Its answer can then come from the text, not from a likely guess
It makes the chatbot type faster
options.why: Speed is not the point; where the answer comes from is.

options.text: It is more polite
options.why: It is about accuracy, not manners.

options.text: A chatbot with the text in front of it is never wrong
options.why: It can still misread, so you check. But it no longer has to recall the text.

feedback.correct: With the text pasted in, the answer can come from it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask where the answer comes from in each case.

explain.text: Asked to recall a document, a model writes likely text about it, which may be invented. With the text pasted in, it can work from the words themselves, and you can check against them.
